2	The second parashah in the book of Vayikra, Parashat Tzav, the Torah
3	here speaks about the altar that was in the Beit HaMikdash.
4	And the Torah says: "And the fire on the altar shall be kept burning, it shall not
5	go out, and the cohen shall kindle wood on it every morning."
6	"And he shall arrange the olah offering on it, and burn on it the fats of the shelamim."
7	"A perpetual fire shall be kept burning on the altar, it shall not go out." There is
8	a repetition here in this verse, in these words: "And the fire
9	on the altar shall be kept burning, it shall not go out." According to the
10	simple meaning, that is how it is. But let us enter a bit into the level of Midrash, the deeper one,
11	to see what is hidden here behind
12	the verses. It is known that the human body is compared to the Beit HaMikdash.
13	Everything that is in the Beit HaMikdash is also in the human body.
14	For example, the Holy
15	of Holies that was in the Beit HaMikdash is actually the brain of
16	man, the place of thoughts. This is the Holy of Holies of
17	man. A person who thinks a forbidden thought, improper reflections,
18	"and you shall not follow after your heart and after
19	your eyes." The Torah commands us: the feeling of the heart
20	and the gaze of the eyes can awaken in him
21	bad thoughts. And the Torah commands a person: do not be
22	like a tourist who wanders after the eyes and the heart. Rule over
23	yourself. See where you look, what you think about, where you
24	end up. When the Torah says, "And the fire on the altar shall be kept burning,
25	it shall not go out," the Torah hints that in a person, in the heart
26	of a Jew, in any situation whatsoever, even if you
27	see that he has fallen to a place where you wonder how
28	he reached such a low point, do not despair of him. Know
29	that in any case "the fire on the altar shall be kept burning, it shall not go out."
30	The Jewish spark is always hidden there in the heart
31	of the person, and this Jewish spark will never
32	go out. You can see in moments of test even a person
33	who testified about himself that he believes in nothing
34	and denies God, yet in moments of test, whether
35	in a time of particular distress or in hours of special emotion,
36	or when he is out in nature and marvels at the beauty of
37	creation, suddenly this spark bursts
38	out again, and you see that in truth there is a fire burning
39	inside him, a pure Jewish fire burning within him. But
40	what is the role of each one of us? To help and assist
41	every Jew. The Torah hints here: "And the fire on the altar
42	shall be kept burning, it shall not go out." Do not despair of any Jew. Know
43	that the Jewish spark always burns within him. "Shall be kept burning on
44	the altar, it shall not go out." There is no chance that it will go out. But "and the cohen
45	shall kindle wood on it every morning." The cohen symbolizes
46	the person who is a teacher of the people, who serves in the Beit
47	HaMikdash, and his role when he is there in the Beit
48	HaMikdash is to add wood in order to fan that same fire
49	that is on the altar, so that the flame will rise. So too
50	every person who has Torah knowledge and is with a person
51	who has not learned and does not know must realize: you are now
52	in the category of the cohen. Your role, as one who knows
53	more, who has learned more: do not say, "Peace upon you, my soul,
54	the main thing is that I'm fine, I have shalom bayit, I enjoy
55	the children, I have my education, I have a good
56	atmosphere at home, respect, Shabbat, tefillin,
57	modesty, kashrut, I am happy
58	with life." Do not content yourself with only yourself. You merited
59	to rise, to receive knowledge, to live a proper life
60	well built. You are happy, so take care of
61	others too. "And the cohen shall kindle wood on it every morning."
62	See how to add wood, how to add knowledge, to
63	the other too. He has his spark, but help him
64	kindle that spark so that it becomes
65	a flame. Without wood it is hard for it to burn. Teach him,
66	inform him. "And he shall arrange the olah offering on it, and burn on it
67	the fats of the shelamim." There is a difference between olah and shelamim.
68	When they brought an olah offering in the Beit HaMikdash, why
69	is this offering called olah? Because all of it
70	went up on the altar; no one ate anything
71	from it, everything goes up on the altar. And shelamim are called
72	shelamim because it makes peace, peace between a person and his fellow,
73	between a person and
74	his Creator. There were types of offerings brought in the Beit
75	HaMikdash where the owner of the sheep also ate of the meat, as did
76	the cohen, and the altar too, everything. This is called shelamim, which
77	connects everyone. It symbolizes the person and his fellow.
78	The olah symbolizes the person and the Almighty, between him and
79	HaShem, and the
80	shelamim symbolize the person and his fellow. That is to say, when
81	you try to help a person, to teach him, guide him
82	both in the mitzvot between him and HaShem and in the mitzvot
83	between him and his fellow, not like those
84	who say, "Learn Kabbalah, for example, and there's no need to keep
85	mitzvot." That is a mistake. How can one teach the Torah against
86	the Torah itself because one wants to please people,
87	so that they will gladly come to classes and learn, and tell them,
88	"You are exempt from all the mitzvot, just come to classes"?
89	Certainly one must not do such a thing. Certainly it is also not
90	appropriate to demand of a person, "If you come to a class, keep
91	the whole Torah." Let him come, learn slowly, decide how
92	he progresses at his own pace, he will rise and grow. But it is a
93	great mistake to convey a message, as I have heard there are such
94	classes, that if you learn Kabbalah then you no longer
95	need the rest of the mitzvot. That is certainly a mistake. Here
96	the Torah teaches a person: when you guide, guide
97	in both tracks, that a person be rectified as far as
98	he is able, both between him and his Maker, between him and
99	HaShem, in the mitzvot between man and the Almighty, and also
100	in the mitzvot between man and his fellow. And therefore it concludes again
101	and says, "A perpetual fire shall be kept burning on the altar, it shall not go out." And so,
102	when a person acts in this way, conveying the message
103	of the Torah also to those around him, to his relatives, acquaintances, friends,
104	then he causes the perpetual fire of the people of Israel, of
105	the Torah itself, to continue for generations upon generations, and thus it will not
106	go out forever and ever, as we were promised in the Torah:
107	"for it shall not be forgotten from the mouth of their descendants." We have a promise in the Torah that
108	this Torah will not be forgotten and will be passed from generation to generation.
109	Our role is to serve as the channels that carry
110	this knowledge, this guidance, on how to enter a
111	good and happy life. Because truly, a person who is not guided
112	according to
113	the Torah not only loses the World to Come, and this is
114	something one sees from experience: if he does whatever
115	he feels like, not according to the manufacturer's instructions, he sees how much
116	he loses in this world. At first it seems that, look, he has
117	pleasures, he does what he feels like, he has no
118	boundaries, he breaks through everywhere.
119	But at a certain stage he reaches a point where he no longer
120	enjoys; he already feels that life has no meaning,
121	he does not find himself. By contrast, when one goes
122	by the manufacturer's instructions, the Torah is in effect telling a person:
123	enjoy everything, but I will put things in order for you: this yes,
124	up to here, here you stop, here you continue, here you return,
125	and so on. The order on the shelves that the Torah arranges for a person
126	along his whole path in life is what gives him
127	happiness and joy and satisfaction and enjoyment, not
128	only in the World to Come but also in this world.
